reason: The text establishes and reinforces hierarchical structures in multiple ways: (1) God's supreme authority over Abram through direct command ('Thus said the LORD unto Abram...'), demonstrating divine hierarchy; (2) Abram's elevated status among humans through being chosen ('I will make of thee a great nation'); (3) A blessing-curse hierarchy based on relationship to Abram ('I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee...all families of the earth shall be blessed in thee'); (4) Implicit hierarchical relationships through the covenant structure where God stands above and selects Abram from among all peoples. While the passage's primary purpose is narrating God's covenant, it fundamentally relies on and implicitly endorses hierarchical ordering—both between God and humanity, and between the chosen individual (Abram) and other humans.
